column3: USD per g of stoichiometric precursor mix
column7: Derived by src/derive.py from Fisher Scientific US list prices fetched 2026-10-10 (catalogue numbers and URLs in the CSV; USD, visible without login; contract prices may be lower) and the routes in data/precursors/routes.csv for our six compositions. Per target, precursors are mixed in stoichiometric mass. Low: cheapest target (Li2MnSiO4) at the largest pack. Base: median target at the smallest pack of >= 100 g. High: dearest target (BaTiS3) at the smallest pack. Rare and transition-metal precursors dominate: In2O3 5.92-10.95 $/g, BaS 10.70-12.80, MnF2 2.96-5.11, against ZnO 0.06-0.33 and Li2CO3 0.37-0.82. The TiSiN2 and BaTiS3 routes are cost proxies (no TiN or TiS2 price). Sigma-Aldrich (A-Lab's supplier) blocked fetching. Not modelled: buying a whole pack for a few grams, which raises cost per attempt for small campaigns.

A-Lab lists its consumables as 'plastic vials, ZrO2 balls and crucibles' and mixes with ethanol and 'ten 5-mm ZrO2 balls'; no costs are published. Base (derived, Fisher US list prices): ethanol 1 mL (ASTRAL robot volume, https://arxiv.org/pdf/2304.00743) at $267.50/L = 0.27; three weighing dishes at $147.50/500 = 0.89; one pair of nitrile gloves at $27.75/100 = 0.56; ten 5-mm YSZ balls, 3.93 g at density 6.0 g/cm3 (assumption) and $246.50/250 g = 3.87 if single use. Low: balls reused, 1.71. High (assumption): 25, for the unpriced items: plastic vials, glovebox consumables for air-sensitive work, agate mortar wear, sieves. XRD sample holders are reused (A-Lab SI) and not charged.

column3: fraction of the indirect-cost base (total direct costs when indirect_base = total_direct)
column4: x F&A base (total direct costs including fees and tuition)
column7: Azoulay, Gross & Sampat (2025), 'Indirect Cost Recovery in U.S. Innovation Policy', NBER WP 33627. Base: the EFFECTIVE indirect cost recovery (ICR) rate, what NIH actually pays, averages 42% (abstract; Table 1, 2024: mean 42%, median 40%, s.d. 10%, min 14%, max 81%). High: the NEGOTIATED ICR rate, the ceiling an institution may charge, averages 58% (abstract; Table 1, 2024: mean 58%, median 56%). Low: 'effective rates in practice are generally between 25% and 45%' (section 3.3, p. 17), lower end. Applying the negotiated 58% would overstate indirect cost by about a third. Population: the underlying data are NIH indirect-cost records for 354 NIH grantee institutions (69% universities, 18% independent hospitals, 13% research institutes; NIH RePORTER since 2006 and the CGAF before), not a census of US universities. The effective rate is NIH ICR paid divided by direct costs for the institution as a whole, a total-direct-cost denominator, whereas the model applies it to an MTDC-like base that excludes tuition and service fees; on a narrower base the true rate per base dollar is somewhat higher, so 42% leans low. Vocabulary: the paper's headline term is 'indirect cost recovery'; it uses 'F&A rate' only for the negotiated agreement. Used only when cost_basis = funder. Base of the charge: labour, fringe, crucibles, precursors and other consumables (MTDC includes salaries, fringe, materials, supplies and services and excludes tuition remission, 2 CFR 200.1, https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/2/200.1). XRD and furnace recharge fees are left out of the base by default: service-centre rates 'must normally consist of its direct costs and an allocable share of all indirect costs' (2 CFR 200.468(b)(2), https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/2/200.468), so indirect cost on top would double-count. Institutional practice varies; choices.fa_base_includes_service_fees reverses this. Negotiated-rate examples, not used: Caltech FY2026 on-campus 70% (https://www.fundingopportunities.caltech.edu/static/guides/FY26_Rate_Memo.pdf), Stanford 54% (FY2025-26), Michigan 56% (FY2025-29), MIT 62% (FY2026). The 2025 NIH 15% cap was vacated (First Circuit, Jan 2026) and is not used.
